name: Password managers
summary: Save a changed password, move the codes to a new phone and help a family member with shared accounts. Where access breaks off between those steps.
lead:
A password manager comes to mind in the middle of something else: you need to open a document, pay for a purchase or help a family member sign in. If the vault does not open, or fills in the old password, the whole job stops. At the same time, making the sign-in simpler must not hide who can reach the entries and under what conditions.

Reviews let you judge how convenient that work is, but not how secure the product is overall. What follows is about observable things: whether the edit was saved, whether the data that was needed came across, and whether the recovery method provided can be followed. Any new solution in this category has to justify its protection model separately.

audiences.title: Update a password and sign in again
audiences.body: After changing a password on a site, a person comes back from a different device. They need the current entry for the right account, not several versions they cannot tell apart.

audiences.title: Move to a new phone
audiences.body: The owner moves across the usernames, codes, notes and files they have built up. The moment that counts is the first successful sign-in, which needs every confirmation method the setup provides.

audiences.title: Help a family member
audiences.body: The job is to open a shared household account or to help with one entry. That kind of help is not the same as access to a person’s whole private archive.

sections.title: Go the full circle of signing in
sections.intro: Find the data, sign in, update the password and open the account again — that is one connected job.

observations.title: Save the entry that was actually updated
passages: Autofill removes the need to look data up and retype it at every sign-in. But that shortcut has to carry on after the password is changed on the site itself. If the new version stayed only in the form, the next sign-in turns back into a manual search for the value that fits.

Saving a new password has to be a visible action. The person sees which entry was updated and can tell a work account from a personal one. If the app requires a manual save, it has to say so clearly while the new value is still available.

An offer to save that comes and goes is especially awkward: a person does not know when they can rely on the familiar step. After a password change there has to be a way at hand to check the entry and sign in again. For a client of your own password file this sequence matters as much as being able to read a compatible format.

This was fairly simple to fix by updating my password, which probably needed to be done anyway. It not only stores my passwords, but promp

placements.title: Save the entry that was actually updated

observations.title: Understand why the sign-in was refused
passages: A repeating biometric prompt, a sign-in refused on one device and a forgotten main password look alike only from the outside: the vault does not open. The causes and the actions available differ. A person needs to understand their own situation, not press the same button again hoping for a different result.

A login loop on one device and a forgotten main password are different situations. If the same credentials open the vault on a computer, repeating them endlessly on the phone is pointless. The interface has to show at which step the refusal came up and which provided alternatives are available, without suggesting risky actions at random.

With a forgotten main password, what recovery is possible depends on how the vault itself is built and on the owner’s settings. That cannot be replaced with a promise that “we will get everything back”. A person needs to know in advance what is held by them alone and what help can be arranged with a family member. This matters especially for a product with a simple interface: simplicity must not hide the limits of recovery.

quotes.text: This app was great until recently. I had dozens of my passwords stored here for home and work. Recently the app was glitching on face recognition mode. Kept going cycling through face recognition over and over. Would not accept it and would not let me put a password in instead.

Master password sometimes flat out fails. App will not accept it but same pass on desktop works, or desktop doesn't but website does. Website frequently also goes into a login loop on mobile and is correct but will not proceed to the actual vault.
It's great until you have lost memory of your main password and then youre Screwed. Im going back to paper and pen.

placements.title: Understand why the sign-in was refused

observations.title: Move from a warning to an action
passages: A warning about a password is useful when it makes clear what happened to a particular entry. Being found in a breach and a strength score are different grounds for attention. A red mark nobody can read leaves a person with anxiety and the extra job of working the terminology out alone.

A strength score needs an explanation separate from a breach notification. One user is surprised that a randomly generated password is judged weak; the review itself does not let you check whether that judgement was sound. The product has to reveal the reason for the mark and tell a recommendation to replace a password apart from information about a particular incident.

A generator becomes useful when the value it offers is saved for the right account and works at the next sign-in. A list of warnings can have an ending just as clear: the person has dealt with a particular entry, not merely opened a red card. A general counter of flags is no substitute for that result.

quotes.text: I was notified that 3 of my passwords were comprised in a data leak!
Apple generated a random password for me, but this app said that "RXF345-BMA-810" would be easy to guess?!??!

Love this app! I love that it syncs all my devices and love that I don't have to try and remember my passwords. The best part is the password generator. It treks me when passwords are weak and creates a new one when I want it to.

art.alt: Illustration for the theme “Going from a warning to an action”.

placements.title: Move from a warning to an action

sections.title: Move access while keeping the contents
sections.intro: Passwords, codes, notes and attachments can each call for different actions. They have to be checked separately.

observations.title: Test the second step on the new device
passages: A one-time code is usually needed in the middle of a sign-in. So an entry that has vanished or is labelled unclearly stops the whole job, even when the password has been found. What matters is a readable link to the service and the account, and a separate check that the codes are available after the device is replaced.

Do not put the password transfer and the second step under one message of success. Let the owner sign in to an account of their choice from the new phone and see which confirmation method is in use. The fallback path provided in advance should be explained for that method, without promising one button for every case.

Even without a change of phone, code entries that have vanished can stop access to other accounts. So the screen has to tell three things apart: an empty vault, data that has not loaded yet, and an unsupported transfer. A new phone counts as ready not after a general sync mark, but after the owner has tested the sign-in methods they need.

quotes.text: This is generally good, but if you forget to migrate things manually before getting a new phone, your accounts are forever lost

Every time I get a new phone, getting my accounts set back up is a nightmare. It wont let you delete and re-add an account. It tries to have you sign in but then it asks for an Authenticator code to complete the sign in process.

I only click into the app to get a code when needed. Logged in one day and every single one of my accounts was no longer there. No codes for anything, and guess what? Now I can't access anything else. DO NOT USE THIS APP

placements.title: Test the second step on the new device

observations.title: Reconcile the archive after the move
passages: Over the years a vault gathers more than usernames and passwords. Next to them there can be notes and photos of documents, useful at the moment the entry is opened. A move that kept only the main fields can therefore look finished before the person discovers what is missing.

The import has to work on the device the person actually has. Instructions to install an extension on a computer help the owner of a single iPhone very little. It matters to name the source formats supported in advance, and to keep separately the pieces for which the new vault has no suitable field.

The way out of a vault matters as much as the way in. If only the old app understands the export, hundreds of entries have to be moved by hand. Passwords, notes and attachments should be checked as different parts of the archive: support for the main fields does not yet guarantee that the documents beside them come across.

The instructions tell you to download another browser that supports the proton extensions, but apple doesn't allow extensions on any t

placements.title: Reconcile the archive after the move

observations.title: Test your own devices and sign-in methods
passages: A manager is used inside a particular setup: a phone, a browser, a work computer, the connection available. A feature can suit you at home and turn out to be awkward where an extension cannot be installed. Passkeys add actions of their own for creating, saving and then signing in.

A break on one platform can make the whole vault awkward. A person keeps the data on a phone but signs in from a work computer; a missing extension or missing passkey support will stop exactly that crossing. Capabilities have to be described for particular devices and sign-in methods, not with one blanket “works everywhere”.

A passkey is a separate way in, not one more password line. An app can read the file perfectly well and still be unable to save a key from the service you need. Choosing your own cloud will not fix that: sign-in support and the storage place are different decisions, and each has to be described precisely.

quotes.text: It's such a massive feature gap to not have support for Passkeys on macOS.
Works well but without passkey support on MacOS and Windows browser extension. It leaves me to shy away from recommending to others.

I've been using this app for a few years now, and even bought the lifetime license. It's been great, except for passkeys. For some reason this app breaks whenever I try to save passkeys from every one of my iOS apps to my db (it both fails to save the key and crashes upon retry).

placements.title: Test your own devices and sign-in methods

sections.title: Help family with boundaries you can see
sections.intro: A shared sign-in, a private archive and access in an exceptional situation must not be mixed together.

observations.title: Separate shared from private
passages: A shared entry is useful to a family when everyone involved has the same current version. Passing copies around gradually raises the question of who changed the password last and where the right one is now. A shared vault has to keep a clear division between the shared material and each person’s private part.

Helping a family member and access in an exceptional situation call for different agreements. Ordinary help needs no more than the entries you pick; wider access has to be agreed separately. Let people see who is involved and who is responsible for updates, then run a familiar action through together, without handing over a whole private archive for the sake of one sign-in.

A shared database has to stay one current history of changes. When a husband and wife end up with copies that differ, it is unclear where the right password is now. That is the everyday job of sharing; opening the archive in an emergency, after the owner’s illness or death, calls for a procedure of its own and must not be switched on unnoticed along with ordinary sharing.

quotes.text: Been using DashLane for 6 years now with 5 family members all using it as well. It seamlessly updates my passwords no matter what platform I'm using. My parents are getting older and sharing passwords and having them on the same platform as me makes thing

As someone in their 40s, not only do I appreciate not having to remember my own passwords, but this app has saved me hours upon hours of tech support for my parents. My dad passed recently and unexpectedly, and being able to access his accounts has made the logistics of death so much easier than it

I love this app and have been using it for years! The only grip I have is my wife and I have found it difficult to share the same database in cloud storage. At various times the databases have gotten out of sync and we have not been able to get them merged back again.

art.alt: Illustration for the theme “Separating shared from personal”.

conclusion.title: Pick a narrow stretch, not a new vault
conclusion.body:
The clearest opportunity in these reviews is helping with the move between particular vaults: showing compatibility in advance, carrying the supported parts across and naming what was left out. But even a tool like that works with secrets, so it cannot be treated as a simple file converter. Before building the product you need competence in protecting data and a clear answer for temporary copies, errors and the deletion of material.

For a team without that preparation I would not choose a password manager as a first product. Improving the interface of an existing, proven solution may make more sense. The value of the move itself can first be judged on a synthetic archive and by watching the current process: where a person gets stuck and what they have to restore by hand.
